title: Reasoning transparency
html:
Why reasoning transparency?

In this course you will make claims about where time and money do the most good. Those claims are easy to get wrong, and getting them wrong matters. Reasoning transparency means showing how you reached a conclusion, not only what it is, so that other people can find the mistake before you act on it. GiveWell and Coefficient Giving publish their reasoning for the same reason, as you will see in Weeks 2 and 3.

How to do it:

  • State your conclusion first. Then explain why.

  • Show your working. What evidence did you consider, and how does it lead to your conclusion?

  • Say how confident you are. “I’d put this at 70%” is more useful than “probably”. Most people are overconfident, and you will practise calibration in Week 3.

  • Name your assumptions. What would have to be true for your reasoning to hold? What would change your mind?

  • Make it checkable. Link to sources and say exactly where a claim comes from.

  • Be honest about limits. “This is based on ten minutes of searching” is useful information.

Practise on a real argument (12 mins)

The case for effective altruism rests on an empirical claim: some ways of doing good achieve far more than others. If they were all about equally good, careful comparison would hardly matter.

Read: Toby Ord, The Moral Imperative toward Cost-Effectiveness in Global Health (12 mins).

Ord argues that health interventions differ in cost-effectiveness by factors of a hundred or more, not by a few per cent. As you read, follow the argument and also notice how well he shows his reasoning. You will rate it in the exercises.

One term you will meet: a DALY (disability-adjusted life year) is a year of healthy life lost to illness or early death. Week 2 covers it properly.

Why this is surprising

One reason is scope insensitivity. In studies, people offered roughly the same amount to save 2,000 birds from an oil spill as to save 200,000. Our feelings don’t scale with the numbers, so we have to check them against the numbers.

What follows

If one option does 100 times more good than another, choosing the merely good option has a cost: the better one you didn’t fund. Economists call this opportunity cost.

This is why large funders set a bar, a minimum amount of good a project must do before they fund it. Coefficient Giving’s bar is roughly one year of healthy life for every $50 it spends. Projects below it usually aren’t funded, even though many would look very cost-effective by ordinary standards.

That can feel uncomfortable, because turning down a good project means someone goes unhelped. The argument for the bar is that funding the good project instead of a much better one leaves more people unhelped. The bar comes back in Weeks 2, 3 and 5.
